name: git branch
shortDescription: List, create, rename, or delete branches. Branches are lightweight, movable pointers to commits that enable parallel lines of development.
detailedDescription:
Branches are one of Git's most powerful features. A branch is simply a named pointer to a specific commit. When you create a branch, Git just creates a new pointer — it doesn't copy any files. This makes branching incredibly fast and cheap, unlike older version control systems.

The `HEAD` pointer tells Git which branch you're currently on. When you commit, the current branch pointer moves forward to the new commit while other branches stay where they are.

**Branching strategies** vary by team:
- **Git Flow**: `main`, `develop`, `feature/*`, `release/*`, `hotfix/*`
- **GitHub Flow**: `main` + short-lived feature branches
- **Trunk-Based**: Everyone commits to `main`, uses feature flags

Remote-tracking branches (like `origin/main`) are read-only references to the state of branches on the remote server. They update when you `fetch` or `pull`.

parameters.description: List all local branches. The current branch is highlighted with an asterisk (*).
Create a new branch pointing at the current commit (HEAD). Does NOT switch to it — use `git checkout -b` or `git switch -c` for that.
List both local and remote-tracking branches.
Delete a branch that has been fully merged. Git refuses to delete unmerged branches with this flag to prevent data loss.
Force-delete a branch regardless of merge status. Use when you're sure you want to discard an unmerged branch's work.
Rename a branch. If you're on the branch you want to rename, you can omit <old>: `git branch -m new-name`.
Show the last commit hash and message for each branch. Use -vv to also show the upstream tracking branch.
Filter branches that have (or haven't) been merged into the current branch. `--merged` is useful for finding branches safe to delete.

examples.title: List all branches
examples.description: See what branches exist locally and which one you're on.
examples.code:
git branch

# Output:
#   develop
# * main
#   feature-auth

# Show all branches including remotes:
git branch -a

examples.title: Create a new feature branch
examples.description: Create a branch from the current position. Note: this doesn't switch to it.
examples.code:
git branch feature-user-profile

# To create AND switch in one command:
git checkout -b feature-user-profile
# or (Git 2.23+):
git switch -c feature-user-profile

examples.title: Delete merged branches (cleanup)
examples.description: After merging feature branches, clean them up to keep your branch list tidy.
examples.code:
# See which branches are already merged:
git branch --merged

# Delete a merged branch:
git branch -d feature-old-login

# Delete all merged branches except main and develop:
git branch --merged | grep -v 'main\|develop' | xargs git branch -d

examples.title: Rename a branch
examples.description: Rename the branch you're currently on, or specify the old name explicitly.
examples.code:
# Rename current branch:
git branch -m new-name

# Rename a different branch:
git branch -m old-name new-name

# After renaming, update the remote:
git push origin -u new-name
git push origin --delete old-name

examples.title: See tracking relationships
examples.description: Check which remote branch each local branch is tracking.
examples.code:
git branch -vv

# Output:
#   develop  a1b2c3d [origin/develop: ahead 2] Add caching
# * main     e4f5g6h [origin/main] Latest release
#   feature  i7j8k9l No upstream configured

commonMistakes.text: `git branch <name>` creates a branch but does NOT switch to it. You'll still be on your current branch. Use `git checkout -b` or `git switch -c` to create + switch.
Using `-D` (uppercase) force-deletes a branch even if it has unmerged work. That work becomes very hard to recover. Always try `-d` first — Git will warn you if there's unmerged work.
Deleting a local branch does NOT delete the remote branch. To delete the remote branch too, run: `git push origin --delete branch-name`.
